column2: Then, having conquered the whole earth, lotus-eyed Rama, the hero, performed a sacrifice honoured by brahmins and kshatriyas.
The horse sacrifice, great king, joined with all desires, purifying all beings and increasing splendour and brightness.
Though sinless and radiant, Jamadagni's son by the fruit of that sacrifice did not feel any lightness of himself.
Having sacrificed with that best sacrifice with ample fees, the great-souled Bhargava asked the sages and gods rich in tradition:
What is the highest purifier for men engaged in fierce deeds? Tell me, greatly fortunate ones, he said, moved to pity. Thus addressed, the great sages who knew the Veda and scriptures said to him:
[Vasishtha said:] "The gods give to those who give gold; for Agni is all the gods, and gold is of his nature.
Therefore all gods are given by one who gives gold, tiger among men; they know nothing higher than this.
Hear also further the greatness of gold, brahmana sage, best of bearers of all weapons, as I tell it.
This was heard by me long ago in the Purana, descendant of Bhrigu, as the Prajapati Manu Svayambhuva was telling it.
When, on the best of mountains, the Himalaya, the blessed trident-bearer, the great-souled Rudra, lifter of Bhrigu's line,
had finished his wedding with the goddess Rudrani, descendant of Bhrigu, at the meeting of the blessed great soul with the goddess, then all the gods, alarmed, approached the blessed one.
Having propitiated Mahadeva seated and the goddess Uma, the boon-giver, with their heads, they all said to Rudra, lifter of Bhrigu's line:
'This union of you, sinless one, with the goddess, ascetic with ascetic, radiant with the radiant, you of unfailing splendour, god of gods, and this goddess Uma,
your offspring, god, will be mighty, lord, and surely in the three worlds will leave nothing remaining.
So give a boon, broad-eyed one, lord of the world, to these gods who bow, wishing the good of the three worlds; restrain your blazing, highest splendour for the sake of offspring.'
As they thus spoke, the blessed bull-bannered one replied to those gods, brahmana sage, "So be it."
Having so said, the bull-rider drew that seed upward, and from then on he was of upward seed.
Then Rudrani, angry at the cutting off of offspring thus done, spoke harsh words to the gods, from a woman's nature:
'Since my husband, desiring offspring, was turned back, therefore all you gods shall be childless.
Since you have today made a cutting-off of my offspring, therefore all of you, sky-goers, will have no offspring.'
Fire was not there at the time of the curse, descendant of Bhrigu; and so the gods, by the goddess's curse, became childless.
Rudra bore the incomparable splendour; but some of it, falling from him, fell on the ground.
It fell then in the fire and grew wonderfully; splendour joined with splendour came to be of one womb.
At this very time the gods led by Shakra were greatly tormented by an asura named Taraka.
The Adityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, Ashvins and Sadhyas were all terrified by the daitya's prowess.
The abodes of the gods, their celestial cars and cities, and the hermitages of the sages were seized by the asuras.
All those gods and sages, with dejected minds, went for refuge to the god Brahma, the ageless lord.
[The gods said:] 'From him fear has arisen for us, grandfather; save us, god, for we have no other goal.'
[Brahma said:] 'I am equal to all beings and do not like unrighteousness here; let Taraka, who harasses the troops of gods and sages, be killed quickly.
The Vedas and dharma must not go to destruction, best of gods; it was arranged by me earlier here; let your fever depart.'
[The gods said:] 'By the blessed one's boon the Daitya is proud of his strength; he cannot be killed by gods; how can he be brought to peace?
He took from you, grandfather, the boon that he be slain by neither gods, nor asuras, nor rakshasas.
And the gods were cursed by Rudrani, when the cutting off of offspring was formerly done: "You will have no offspring," lord of all the world.'
[Brahma said:] 'Fire was not there at the time of the curse, best of gods; he will beget an offspring for the slaying of the gods' enemies.
That, surpassing all gods, danavas and rakshasas, men, gandharvas, nagas and birds,
that splendour, Agni, a great being, as a second fire, will produce in the Ganga for the slaying of the gods' enemies.
That eater of offerings did not receive that curse, being lost then; therefore the son of Pavaka, a remover of your fear, will be born, gods.
Let fire be sought and employed today; the means of slaying Taraka has been told by me, sinless ones.
Curses do not prevail over the radiant; strengths do not become strengths when they meet greater strength.
He could kill even the unkillable and boon-granted ascetics; desire, delighting in resolve, the eternal tamas, the fire;
the lord of the world, indescribable, all-pervading, cherisher of all, dwelling in the heart of all beings, eldest, a lord even above Rudra.
Let him be sought quickly, the mass of splendour, Hutashana; that god will accomplish your desire in mind.'
Hearing this word, the great-souled gods, with their resolve accomplished, went seeking Vibhavasu.
Then the sages with the gods searched the three worlds, wishing to see fire, all with their minds set on it.
Joined with supreme austerity, glorious, famed in the world, all those perfected ones, lifter of Bhrigu's line, roamed the worlds, but did not find Hutashana, lost, merged in himself.
Then a frog, a water-dweller, weary in mind and heated by fire's splendour, risen from the bottom of the nether world, said to the gods who were alarmed and longing to see Agni:
'Lord gods, Agni lives at the bottom of the nether world; I have come here tormented by the heat of Pavaka.
The blessed bearer of offerings sleeps in the water, gods; having mingled the waters with his splendours, we are tormented.
If you, gods, wish to see Vibhavasu, go to him there, if you have business with fire.'
'Go; we shall accomplish it; we, gods, are afraid of fire.' Having said so, the frog quickly entered the water.
But Hutashana learned of the frog's informing; he approached and cursed him: 'You will not know tastes.'
Having joined the frog with the curse, Pavaka went elsewhere to live, the lord, and did not show himself to the gods.
But the gods showed favour to the frogs, descendant of Bhrigu; hear that, mighty-armed one, as I tell it fully.
[The gods said:] 'Though tongueless by Agni's curse and outcast from knowing tastes, you will utter many kinds of Sarasvati.
Gone to live in holes, without taking food, senseless, even dead and dry, the earth will support you; and even in the dark night you will move about.'
Having so spoken to them, the gods went again over this earth for Agni and did not find Hutashana.
Then a certain elephant, like Indra's elephant, said to the gods, descendant of Bhrigu, 'Agni is in the ashvattha.'
Fire, faint with anger, cursed all elephants: 'Your tongue will be reversed,' descendant of Bhrigu.
Having said so, Agni, indicated by the elephant, came out of the ashvattha and entered the womb of the shami tree, wishing to sleep.
Hear the favour that the gods, pleased and truly valiant, did to the elephants, lord, best of Bhrigu's line.
[The gods said:] 'Even with a reversed tongue you will eat everything, and you will utter speech loudly, with indistinct syllables.' Having said so, the dwellers of heaven again followed Agni.
Fire came out of the ashvattha and was in the womb of the shami; reported by a parrot, brahmana, the gods ran to him.
Agni cursed the parrot: 'You will be devoid of speech'; and Hutashana also turned his tongue.
Seeing Agni, the gods, moved by pity, said to the parrot: 'You will not be utterly speechless, bird.
With a tongue turned, your speech will be charming, like a child's or a grown one's, sweet and indistinct, wonderful.'
Having said so, the gods, perceiving fire in the womb of the shami, made it a holy seat for all rites.
From then on, fire is seen in the wombs of shami, and men followed the method of production.
The waters in the nether world mingled with fire, Bhargava, release heat in mountain streams, heated by the splendour of Pavaka lying there.
Then Agni, seeing the gods, was troubled; Pavaka asked them, 'What is the reason for your coming?'
All the gods and the supreme sages said to him: 'We shall employ you in a task; you ought to do it, and when it is done there will be a great merit for you too.'
[Agni said:] 'Say what your task is, gods; I shall do all of it; I am to be employed by you; let there be no doubt for you in this.'
[The gods said:] 'An asura named Taraka, proud of Brahma's boon, harasses us by his might; let his death be ordained.
Save these hosts of gods, hosts of lords of creatures and the greatly fortunate sages, Pavaka.
Beget an offspring joined with splendour, a chief hero, lord, who may destroy the fear we have from the asura, bearer of offerings.
For us, cursed by the great goddess, there is no other refuge than your power; therefore save us.'
Thus addressed, saying 'So be it', the blessed eater of offerings to gods and ancestors, unassailable, went to the Ganga Bhagirathi.
She too became mixed with him, and an embryo was in her; the embryo grew then, like a black-bellied thing, in her side.
By the splendour of that embryo the Ganga's mind was perplexed; she reached great torment and could not bear it.
When the embryo joined with splendour was placed by Fire, an asura in the Ganga let out a terrible cry.
By that great cry which fell without warning, the Ganga, terrified, her eyes wandering and rolling, lost consciousness and could not hold the embryo by herself.
The Jahnavi, her body filled with splendour and trembling, said, brahmana, urged by the strength of the embryo: 'I am not able, blessed one, to bear this splendour.
I am bewildered by this, and great ill health has been made; I am agitated, blessed one, and my splendour is lost, sinless one.
I am not able to bear this embryo, best of the heated; I shall cast it out of sorrow, not at all from desire.
I have no touch of mind, god Vibhavasu; the connection is for calamity, though very subtle, greatly radiant one.
Whatever is here of quality or otherwise, Hutashana, I regard it in you alone; and dharma and adharma alone.'
Fire said to her, 'Bear, bear this embryo joined with my splendour, with great fruits of good qualities.
You are able to bear and hold the whole earth; there is nothing unattainable for you except bearing my seed.'
Restrained by Fire and by the gods, the best of rivers cast that embryo on Meru, the best of mountains.
Though capable of bearing, assailed by Rudra's splendour, she could not bear that embryo by her power.
She cast it out in sorrow, shining like blazing Vaishvanara; and Agni showed himself to her, Ganga, descendant of Bhrigu, and asked the best of rivers, 'Is the embryo well-born?
Of what colour, goddess, and of what form is it seen, joined with what splendour? Tell me all this.'
[Ganga said:] 'That embryo is golden, with splendour like you, Agni; golden, spotless, blazing, it lit the mountain.
Its smell, best of the heated, is cool like lakes mixed with lotuses and water lilies, equal to kadamba flowers.
By the splendour of that embryo, like the rays of the sun, whatever substance on earth or in mountains was touched, all of it was seen turned to gold on every side.
It ran over mountains, rivers and streams and lit the three worlds, moving and unmoving, with its splendour.
Such is your blessed son, bearer of offerings, like sun and fire in brightness, like a second moon in beauty.' Having so spoken, the goddess vanished right there.
And the radiant Pavaka, having done the gods' work, went then to the place he wished, descendant of Bhrigu.
By these deeds and qualities the name of Agni is sung in the world as Hiranyaretas, by sages and gods, and the earth goddess became famed as Vasumati.
That embryo of great splendour, Gangeya, born of Pavaka, reaching the divine reed-thicket, grew, wonderful to see.
The Krittikas saw him, with splendour like the young sun, and with affection arisen nourished that child with streams of milk from their breasts.
Then he, of supreme radiance, gained the name Kartikeya; from being fallen, Skanda; and from living in a cave, Guha.
Thus gold arose as the offspring of Jatavedas; there the best Jambunada became an ornament even of the gods.
From then on this was called Jatarupa; the blessed Agni, the lord, the Prajapati, is gold.
Gold is the purifier of purifiers, best of the twice-born; and Jatarupa is said to be of the nature of Agni and Soma.
It is the best of jewels, the best of ornaments, a purifier of purifiers and auspicious of the auspicious.
Of the great god, dear one, bearing the body of Varuna, in the lordship of Varuna, Rama, of Rudra the lord, lord,
all the sages and the gods led by Agni came, and all the parts of sacrifice, and the vashat-cry embodied.
Samans embodied and Yajus by the thousand, and the Rig Veda came there adorned with the pada and krama recitations.
The marks, accents, stobhas, Nirukta and the divisions of accent, and Om dwelt in his eyes, along with restraint and grasp.
The Vedas with the Upanishads, knowledge and the Savitri; the blessed Shiva bore past, present and future, and then offered himself in himself, lord.
The wives of the gods, the maidens and the mothers of the gods came together there then, lifter of Bhrigu's line.
Delighted at the sacrifice of the lord of beasts and the great-souled Varuna, the Self-born, seeing them, let his seed fall on the ground.
From the flowing of that seed, Pushan, gathering dust from the ground, threw it with both hands into that same fire.
Taking that seed, just fallen, with the ladle, he offered it with mantra like ghee, descendant of Bhrigu.
Then the mighty one produced the host of beings; from that splendour, in the worlds, what is fiery was born.
From tamas, tamasic states; sattva pervaded; and both: the quality of splendour is always, and of tamas, space.
In all beings, then, sattva, splendour and tamas; when the seed was offered in that fire, three appeared, lord,
men with bodies, joined with qualities born of birth. He was called Bhrigu because of "Bhrigu"; Angiras arose from the embers.
From taking refuge in embers another, Kavi, arose; Bhrigu, born with the flames, is remembered as Bhrigu.
From rays, Marichi; Marichi's son was Kashyapa; from the embers Angiras, dear one; the Valakhilyas from a heap of rock; and Atri, born right there, they also say, lord.
And from the removal of ash arose the Vaikhanasas, equal to the group of Brahmarishis, wishing the qualities of austerity and learning; and from his hearing the two Ashvins, approved in form, arose.
The other lords of creatures were born from his streams, the sages from the wells of the world, and the metres from sweat and impurity.
For this reason they call Agni all the gods; sages rich in learning say so, seeing the authority of the Veda.
The logs are the months, the sap is called the fortnights; the days and nights are the moments, and bile and light are Varuna's.
Red they call Rudra's; from red gold is remembered; know that as Mitra's; and from smoke the Vasus are remembered.
Those who are flames are the Rudras and the Adityas of great splendour; the embers are indicated as those standing in the hearths in heaven.
And lord of the world, the supreme Brahman, fixed; they call it the giver of all desires; there he carried the offering.
Then Mahadeva Varuna, the supreme Self, said: 'This divine sacrificial session is mine; I am the householder here.
The first three offspring are mine, without doubt; know this, sky-goers, for that is the fruit of my sacrifice.'
[Agni said:] 'They were born from my limbs and made in my shelter; those offspring are mine alone; Varuna is of helpless nature.'
Then Brahma, teacher of the world, grandfather of the world, said: 'Those offspring are mine alone, for my seed was offered.
I am the speaker of the mantra and the hotri of the seed; whose seed is the fruit is his, if the seed is held to be the cause.'
Then the hosts of gods, approaching the grandfather with joined palms and bowing their heads, said:
'And we all, blessed one, and the world with moving and unmoving, are your issue; therefore Agni is Vibhavasu; and Varuna the lord and god, let him receive his desired wish.'
By nature Varuna, lord of waters, took Bhrigu first, an offspring of sun-like splendour, of Brahma.
Ishvara appointed Angiras as Agni's offspring, and the grandfather, knowing the truth, took Kavi as offspring.

Then Bhrigu was famed as Varuna's, the maker of begetting; Angiras, glorious, Agni's; and Kavi, of great fame, Brahma's; Bhargava and Angiras in the world have the mark of continuing the world's line.
These three best brahmanas, lords of creatures: know that all the line is of these.
Bhrigu's seven sons there were equal to Bhrigu in qualities: Chyavana, Vajrashirsha, Shuchi, Aurva,
Shukra, Varenya, Vibhu and Savana: those seven Bhargavas, all Varuna's, in whose line you also are.
Eight sons of Angiras are also told as Varuna's: Brihaspati, Utathya, Vayasya, Shanti,
Ghora, Virupa, Samvarta and Sudhanva as the eighth; these eight, all Agni-born, are devoted to knowledge and free of ill.
The sons of the brahmana Kavi are also said to be Varuna's, eight, knowers of Brahman, auspicious, joined with qualities born of birth.
Kavi, Kavya, Vishnu, the wise Ushanas, Bhrigu, Viraja, Kashi, and the dharma-knowing Ugra.
These are the eight sons of Kavi; by them the whole world is spread; these are the lords of creatures through whom these creatures are.
Thus by the descendants of Angiras and Kavi, and by those of Bhrigu, tiger of Bhrigus, the world is continually.
Varuna, brahmana, the lord, took Kavi and Bhrigu from Aditi; therefore those two are remembered as Varuna's.
The crested god took Angiras; therefore Hutashana; therefore Angiras and all his line are to be known as such.
The grandfather Brahma, formerly propitiated by the gods: 'These will carry us across with their offspring, lords of the world.
All lords of creatures, all great ascetics; by your grace they will carry this eternal world across.'
Likewise the makers of lines, increasers of your splendour, will be knowers of the Veda and masters of speech.
Bearers of the gods' side, gentle, great sages of Prajapati, they gain austerity and supreme celibacy.
All we and these are your issue, lord; you are the maker of gods and brahmanas, grandfather.
Making Marichi first, and all the Bhargavas, seeing them as offspring, forgive, grandfather.
In this very form they will beget offspring and establish themselves at the beginning and end of ages.
Thus this ancient event occurred at the sacrifice of that great soul, best of gods, at the beginning of the world, bearing Varuna's body.
Agni, Brahma, Pashupati, Sharva, Rudra and Prajapati: this gold is Agni's offspring; so the conception stands.
In the absence of Agni they place gold in fire-places, knowers of the authority of Jamadagni's rule, from the illustration of the Veda.
One offers to Agni in a bunch of kusha grass, the gold placed there; in the offering the blessed one thinks of prosperity as pleasing.
Therefore we have heard that all gods are devoted to Agni; Agni is born of Brahma, and gold of Agni.
Therefore those seers of dharma who give gold, we have heard, give all the gods.
His worlds, going to the highest goal, free of darkness, in heaven he will be consecrated with kingship of kings, Bhargava.
When the sunrise has come, one who gives gold with rule and mantras destroys a bad dream.
One who gives at sunrise has his sin shaken off; giving gold at midday kills sin to come.
One who gives gold at evening twilight, firm in vow, goes to the same world as Brahma, wind, fire and Soma.
He gains good foundation in the worlds with Indra; gaining fame in this world, with sin appeased, he rejoices.
Then in other worlds he is always incomparable, of unobstructed course, going at will.
And he does not decline from them and constantly gains the great; having given imperishable gold, he gains abundant worlds.
One who, having kindled fire, gives for a vow toward sunrise, attains all desires.
They call it Agni; the gift brings happiness, joined with desired qualities, remembered as a promoter.
[Bhishma said:] Thus addressed by Vasishtha, the mighty Jamadagni's son gave gold to brahmanas and was freed from stain.
All this has been told to you, lord of the earth, of gold, the fruit of giving it, and its birth from Agni, unsurpassed.
Therefore you too give much gold to brahmanas; giving gold, king, you will be freed from stain.
[Yudhishthira said:] The cause of the origin of gold was told here; how then did Taraka meet his death? Tell me that.
It was said by the gods that he could not be killed, lord of the earth, but his death was not told to you in detail.
I wish to hear this from you, lifter of the Kuru line, the full account of Taraka's killing; my curiosity is great.
[Bhishma said:] When their work had failed, king of kings, gods and sages urged the Krittikas to bear offspring.
Of the gods' wives, not one was able, even a single one, to hold that embryo by her power.
Then Pavaka was pleased with those six for bearing the embryo, by release of his own splendour and by supreme power.
Those six Krittikas nourished the embryo of Jatavedas; the whole splendour of fire was placed in six paths, lord.
Then, as the great-souled boy grew, they, their limbs filled with his splendour, found no comfort anywhere.
Then the earth received that embryo, with six supports, come to oneness, near the city of Kanti.
That embryo of divine form, radiant, bright as Pavaka, reaching the divine reed-thicket, grew, pleasing to see.
The Krittikas saw that child, bright like fire, and out of affection and friendship nourished him with streams of milk from their breasts.
He became Kartikeya in the three worlds with moving and unmoving; from being fallen, Skanda, and from living in a cave, Guha.
Then the thirty-three gods and the lords of directions with the directions, Rudra, Dhatri and Vishnu, Yajna, Pushan, Aryaman, Bhaga,
Amsha, Mitra and the Sadhyas, the Vasus, Vasava and the Ashvins, water, wind, space, moon, stars, planets and sun,
and other separate beings who are offerings to the gods, came there to see that boy, the son of fire; the sages praised and the gandharvas sang.
Six-faced, twelve-eyed, dear to brahmanas, broad-shouldered, twelve-armed, of splendour like fire and sun, that boy,
lying in the reed thicket, seen by the gods with the sages, they gained supreme joy and thought the asura slain.
Then all the gods did what was dear to him, giving playthings for him at play, and flocks of birds.
Suparna gave him a feather and the peacock with its coloured tail, and the rakshasas gave the boar and the buffalo.
Varuna himself gave a cock like fire, the moon gave a ram, and the sun a lovely radiance.
The goddess mother of cows gave cows by the hundred thousand, Agni a goat with good qualities, and Ila abundant flowers and fruit.
Sudhanva gave a cart and a chariot with endless poles; Varuna gave lovely divine serpents of Varuna; the lord of the gods gave lions, tigers, leopards and other fanged beasts,
and many fierce wild animals and various parasols; and the hosts of rakshasas and asuras who followed that lord.
Seeing him grow, Taraka sought by many means to kill that lord, but could not.
The gods, honouring him with generalship, told him of the injury done by Taraka, as he lived in the cave.
Grown, of great prowess, the lord Guha, general of the gods, killed the danava Taraka with his unfailing spear.
When the asura was killed by that boy at play, the lord of the gods was set in the kingdom, again lord of the gods.
Follow him from behind wherever that mighty one goes; having reached him in solitude, take refuge with joined palms.
Thus addressed, he, Vyasa, best of upholders of dharma, of great splendour, spoke again to Yudhishthira, lord of men.
Then, having praised Govinda and told the Pandava's story, he comforted those women and went to see his maternal uncle.
Or is their place there eternal, best of the twice-born, or have those bulls among men gone to some other goal by their deeds? I wish to hear this told by you, twice-born.
